query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Removing Co from the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy increases the amplitude and spatial variation of local Peierls friction barriers, which in turn leads to more uniformly distributed dislocation pinning. This modified pinning behavior enables the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy to maintain an optimal strength–ductility balance across a range of temperatures and strain rates.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified solid-solution FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy derived by removing Co from the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi composition.
generation.intervention: Eliminate Co from the alloy system (i.e., substitute the CoCrFeMnNi alloy with a Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy) to modify the local solute field.
generation.conditions: Test across a temperature range from room temperature up to high temperatures (e.g., 1000 °C) and over a spectrum of strain rates under controlled, non-segregated, solid-solution conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local fluctuations in the Peierls friction barrier arising from altered chemical disorder in the absence of Co.
generation.mechanism: Without Co, the altered solute–dislocation interaction increases the magnitude and distribution of local Peierls barriers. This promotes intermittent yet more uniformly distributed dislocation pinning and glide, resulting in an enhanced work-hardening response that preserves both strength and ductility even as temperature and strain rate vary.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in work-hardening behavior and a moderated flow stress escalation at high temperatures and strain rates, reflecting a broader distribution of dislocation pinning events.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy (with Co present) under the same processing and testing conditions.
generation.boundary: Applicable only to alloys processed into homogeneous, non-segregated single-phase solid solutions without secondary phase precipitations, and within the tested temperature (RT to ~1000 °C) and strain rate regimes.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence linking the absence of Co to enhanced local Peierls friction fluctuations is limited, so the magnitude of its effect on dislocation behavior and work-hardening remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy variants: one with the conventional equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi composition and one Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy. Conduct in-situ transmission electron microscopy studies during mechanical tests, spanning various temperatures (room temperature to ~1000 °C) and strain rates. Measure dislocation glide behavior, especially the spatial distribution and density of pinning events. Concurrently, perform macro-scale mechanical tests (e.g., compression or tensile tests) to extract work-hardening rates, yield strengths, and ductility.
measurements: Quantitative mapping of dislocation pinning site density and distribution (as a proxy for local Peierls friction fluctuations)
Dislocation glide mobility and jerky motion characteristics measured via in-situ TEM
Work-hardening rate and yield strength from mechanical testing
Comparative ductility measurements (plastic strain to failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in the spatial variation of dislocation pinning (i.e., local Peierls barrier fluctuations) and does not exhibit the predicted modifications in work-hardening behavior and ductility relative to the baseline alloy, then this hypothesis would be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractDislocations in single-phase concentrated random alloys, including high-entropy alloys (HEAs), repeatedly encounter pinning during glide, resulting in jerky dislocation motion. While solute-dislocation interaction is well understood in conventional alloys, the origin of individual pinning points in concentrated random alloys is a matter of debate. In this work, we investigate the origin of dislocation pinning in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA. In-situ transmission electron microscopy studies reveal wavy dislocation lines and a jagged glide motion under external loading, even though no segregation or clustering is found around Shockley partial dislocations. Atomistic simulations reproduce the jerky dislocation motion and link the repeated pinning to local fluctuations in the Peierls friction. We demonstrate that the density of high local Peierls friction is proportional to the critical stress required for dislocation glide and the dislocation mobility.Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Structural properties Dislocations in high-entropy alloys encounter pinning during glide resulting in jerky motion.
